issue.title: Gemini Interactions API surface (/v1beta/interactions) with Responses translation

type.name: Feature
type.description: A request, idea, or new functionality

issue.body:
Part of #720 (sub-issue). Case study: [docs/case-studies/issue-720](https://github.com/link-assistant/router/blob/issue-720-99e7abc4e6c1/docs/case-studies/issue-720/README.md).

Blocked by: #725 (declared with GitHub issue dependencies).

## Summary
Newer Gemini CLI builds use the Gemini Interactions API (`/v1beta/interactions`) in addition to `v1beta/models/*:generateContent`. CLIProxyAPI routes it natively and translates it from and to OpenAI Responses (`internal/translator/{openai,gemini}/interactions`). Router has no such route.

Blocked by the canonical thinking pipeline, because the interactions matrix (`TestThinkingE2EMatrix_InteractionsMatrix`) depends on it.

Case study: `docs/case-studies/issue-720/solution-plans.md` § D1.

## Proposal
1. Route `/api/services/gemini/v1beta/interactions` (and streaming variant) natively to Gemini with the existing `x-goog-api-key` / `GEMINI_API_KEY` / imported-credential handling.
2. Translate OpenAI Responses ↔ Interactions so Codex-dialect clients can reach Gemini and Gemini CLI can reach Responses providers, subject to the subscription-bridge policy.
3. Apply thinking through the canonical pipeline.

## Tests
Native relay (headers, streaming, error passthrough); translation fixtures ported from CLIProxyAPI translator tests; thinking interactions matrix.

## Prior art
CLIProxyAPI `internal/translator/openai/interactions/responses/*_test.go`, `internal/translator/gemini/interactions/*_test.go`.

## Compatibility
Additive route.

issue.title: Translator conformance suite ported from CLIProxyAPI test corpora
issue.body:
Part of #720 (sub-issue). Case study: [docs/case-studies/issue-720](https://github.com/link-assistant/router/blob/issue-720-99e7abc4e6c1/docs/case-studies/issue-720/README.md).

Blocked by: #725 #729 (declared with GitHub issue dependencies).

## Summary
CLIProxyAPI has roughly 100 translator test files covering OpenAI↔Claude, OpenAI↔Gemini, Codex↔Claude, Antigravity and Interactions conversions. Their table-driven vectors are MIT licensed and transfer directly. Router's bridge tests cover fewer cases.

Blocked by the canonical thinking pipeline and the Gemini Interactions route, which the corpora exercise.

Case study: `docs/case-studies/issue-720/test-reuse.md`.

## Proposal
1. An extraction script under `experiments/` that takes an upstream checkout path as an argument, extracts vectors from the listed Go test files into JSON fixture pairs, and never executes anything from the checkout.
2. Load the pairs with Router's recorded-fixture harness (#671) as tier-1 tests, one file per protocol pair, attributed in the header.
3. Document how to refresh the corpus against a newer upstream tag.

## Tests
The ported corpora themselves; a self-test that the extractor output is stable.

## Prior art
CLIProxyAPI `internal/translator/**/*_test.go`, `test/builtin_tools_translation_test.go`, `test/summary_intent_translation_test.go`.

issue.title: Port CLIProxyAPI cross-module regression suites (sentinel, built-in tools, parallel calls, disconnect failover, usage logging)
issue.body:
Part of #720 (sub-issue). Case study: [docs/case-studies/issue-720](https://github.com/link-assistant/router/blob/issue-720-99e7abc4e6c1/docs/case-studies/issue-720/README.md).

Blocked by: #725 #724 #738 (declared with GitHub issue dependencies).

## Summary
CLIProxyAPI's `test/` directory holds cross-module regression suites that encode behaviours clients depend on: Claude Code compatibility sentinel, built-in tools translation, Codex↔Claude parallel function calls, stream-disconnect failover, usage logging, summary/intent translation. Router covers some of these indirectly; porting them makes the coverage explicit.

Blocked by the canonical thinking pipeline, model-level cooldowns, and the translator conformance suite.

Case study: `docs/case-studies/issue-720/test-reuse.md`.

## Proposal
Port each suite as a Router tier-1/2 test with a mock upstream and a controllable clock, keeping the upstream assertions and attributing the source file:
- `claude_code_compatibility_sentinel_test.go` → extend the Claude Code feature matrix (#675)
- `builtin_tools_translation_test.go`, `codex_claude_parallel_function_calls_test.go`, `summary_intent_translation_test.go` → bridge tests
- `codex_stream_disconnect_failover_test.go` → pool failover tests
- `usage_logging_test.go` → usage attribution tests

## Tests
The ported suites; each must fail against a deliberately broken bridge to prove it bites.

## Prior art
CLIProxyAPI `test/*.go` (9 files).

issue.title: docs: case study and sub-issue plan for CLIProxyAPI feature parity (#720)
issue.body:
Issue #720 asks for a deep analysis of CLIProxyAPI, a case study under `docs/case-studies/issue-720`, a list of every requirement with solution plans, a survey of existing components, reuse of as many upstream tests as possible, and sub-issues with GitHub blockers that deliver the work. This PR delivers the analysis and the issue breakdown; the code lands through the sub-issues.

### Case study

[docs/case-studies/issue-720/](https://github.com/link-assistant/router/blob/issue-720-99e7abc4e6c1/docs/case-studies/issue-720/README.md) compares CLIProxyAPI v8.0.20 (commit `0f96f568`, 918 test files) with Router v1.18.3:

- [README.md](https://github.com/link-assistant/router/blob/issue-720-99e7abc4e6c1/docs/case-studies/issue-720/README.md): scope, snapshot, gap summary, reliability/security/safety analysis, issue plan.
- [requirements.md](https://github.com/link-assistant/router/blob/issue-720-99e7abc4e6c1/docs/case-studies/issue-720/requirements.md): 15 requirements traced from the issue text plus 4 implicit repository requirements, each with a solution and a verification.
- [feature-matrix.md](https://github.com/link-assistant/router/blob/issue-720-99e7abc4e6c1/docs/case-studies/issue-720/feature-matrix.md): ~110 rows across protocol surfaces, providers, routing, thinking, management, platform and tests, each with a Have/Partial/Gap/Skip verdict and the sub-issue that closes it.
- [online-research.md](https://github.com/link-assistant/router/blob/issue-720-99e7abc4e6c1/docs/case-studies/issue-720/online-research.md): releases v8.0.11–v8.0.20, documentation mirrors (routing, advanced configuration, management API security), cliproxy-rs, the management center, and ~30 ecosystem tools.
- [components-survey.md](https://github.com/link-assistant/router/blob/issue-720-99e7abc4e6c1/docs/case-studies/issue-720/components-survey.md): crates already in `Cargo.toml` and candidates per gap area, with decisions.
- [solution-plans.md](https://github.com/link-assistant/router/blob/issue-720-99e7abc4e6c1/docs/case-studies/issue-720/solution-plans.md): options, chosen plan, tests and security notes per sub-issue, plus an out-of-scope table with reasons.
- [test-reuse.md](https://github.com/link-assistant/router/blob/issue-720-99e7abc4e6c1/docs/case-studies/issue-720/test-reuse.md): which upstream suites to port as vectors, scenarios or intent, and which not to.
- `raw/`: verbatim MIT-licensed upstream documents (README, config example, management API v8, AGENTS.md, LICENSE), extracted route list and test inventory, and the issue JSON.

### Sub-issues and blockers

Twenty sub-issues (#722–#741) are attached to #720 through the sub-issue API; 21 dependency edges are declared with GitHub `blocked_by`. First wave (unblocked): #722 management hardening, #723 per-credential routing policy, #724 model-level cooldowns and retry budgets, #725 canonical thinking pipeline, #726 provider onboarding contract, #727 catalog sources. The dependency table is in README § 6. Closed issues #668–#684 are referenced, not duplicated; open #718/#719 block the observability issue #728.

### Security and safety decisions recorded

Fingerprint "cloaking" and dynamic-library plugins are out of scope; management hardening (#722) blocks the configuration CRUD (#730) and credential lifecycle (#731) issues; configuration reads redact secrets by default; header passthrough is allow-list only; Router's upstream timeout policy from #669 is kept.

### Validation

`rust-script scripts/check-terminology.rs`, `rust-script scripts/check-file-size.rs` and `cargo fmt --check` pass locally. The change is documentation only, plus a patch changelog fragment. The latest default branch is included.

Part of #720. The parent stays open as the tracking issue for #722–#741.

issue.title: feat: add canonical thinking controls and model suffixes
issue.body:
Requests such as `exact-model(high)` and `exact-model(8192)` now route and authorize the exact base model and apply the requested thinking mode in the destination protocol. Previously, suffixes reached providers as part of the model ID, while several cross-protocol adapters rejected reasoning controls.

Closes #725.

- Add canonical `Off`, `Auto`, `Budget(u32)` and six effort levels, suffix parsing, body extraction, validation and Anthropic, OpenAI Chat/Responses, Gemini/Vertex, Codex and Qwen appliers.
- Normalize HTTP requests, Gemini native URL selectors, every Responses WebSocket `response.create`, and wrapper model grants. Account-policy aliases and prefixes resolve the base identity while preserving suffix intent; grants remain attached to the native upstream model. Response validation compares the exact base model and continues to reject sibling substitutions.
- Apply capability constraints after selecting each account, including HTTP retries and every Codex WebSocket turn. Policy retries restore the original controls before validating the next account, independently of signed/encrypted history stripping. Evidence must match the exact model, account, endpoint, protocol and current credential generation; stale or unknown facts preserve caller intent. Match the actual serialized discovery protocols and retain the original Gemini source through internal bridges. Conversion, clamp and unsupported-drop diagnostics use debug logging.
- Publish optional catalog `thinking` metadata through the strict OpenAPI contract and generated JavaScript/Python types. Unrelated undocumented model properties remain invalid.
- Preserve explicit body precedence, existing Anthropic effort budgets/output headroom, adapter defaults, summary visibility and established signature/encrypted-history replay. Standalone appliers do not register new inference routes or infer capabilities from model names.
- Document grammar and model-truth behavior, and add the minor-release changelog fragment used by automatic releases.

Reproduce and verify:

```console
cargo test --locked --test thinking_pipeline_test --test thinking_parser_test \
  --test thinking_evidence_test --test thinking_matrix_test --test router_e2e_test \
  --test contract_inventory_test --test thinking_account_policy_test \
  --test account_routing_policy_http_test --test account_routing_policy_test
```

The initial three adapter regressions failed before implementation: an Anthropic suffix remained in the model without its budget, Chat reasoning was rejected by Gemini, and Gemini budgets were rejected by Chat. Additional regressions cover manual Anthropic budgets, malformed containers, evidence scope, native Qwen/Vertex controls, exact served identity, HTTP body precedence, signed history and successive WebSocket events. A separate regression first proved that an authenticated unsupported-thinking catalog constrained HTTP but was bypassed by WebSocket ingress; both WebSocket turns now use the same selected-account validator.

The catalog contract regression first failed with `Additional properties are not allowed ('thinking' was unexpected)`. It verifies that authenticated thinking metadata fits the published response contract while an unrelated undocumented field is rejected.

Additional request-based regressions cover trusted legacy reasoning-level metadata, unsupported-control removal across all seven targets, partial/conflicting facts, native Qwen budget errors and suffix clamping, Gemini snake/camel-case precedence and URL selectors, and Anthropic output limits, adaptive auto and historical output headroom.

The account-policy regressions first reproduced suffix aliases returning 403, a budget dropped by the first account remaining absent on retry, failure to clamp a suffix independently for the next account, and an invalid explicit retry budget returning 200 instead of 400. Seven HTTP cases now verify aliases/prefixes and native grants, per-account retry constraints, signature stripping, Codex translation, compressed native retries retaining summary controls, and encoded Gemini selectors with body precedence. Separate failing regressions reproduced discovery's `open_a_i_chat`/`open_a_i_responses` scope mismatch and a Gemini-to-Codex bridge treating translated suffix controls as native body input. All 47 policy and thinking-evidence cases pass together.

All 285 vectors from five CLIProxyAPI v8.0.20 matrices are retained with the pinned revision, upstream MIT license and a regeneration script. Three property tests each run 128 bounded cases. Router intentionally retains body precedence and does not add the upstream default in the shared pipeline; existing adapter defaults remain.

Local validation passes all 2,181 Linux unit tests, 922 integration cases across 123 targets, all 15 documentation tests, the independent Rust library consumer and all 27 real-binary binding cases (nine each in Node, Bun and Python). The existing soak test runs in its dedicated CI workflow. Unit tests use exhaustive temporary partitions under a finite memory bound because this workspace has 3 GB RAM; production source is retained and every Linux unit entry point runs once. One compilation partition exceeded the bound before tests and passed after subdivision, covering the same 261 tests.

Strict all-target/all-feature Clippy, formatting, TypeScript, generated contract/binding parity, backward compatibility, vendor fixtures, file-size and terminology checks pass. All fourteen automation script suites, release preparation/retry tests, remote checkpoint contracts and workflow invariants pass. The branch includes current main's v1.22.0 release metadata and retains the minor changelog fragment for the next release. The metadata sync changes no application or test source; 87 focused integration cases across eight version-sensitive targets and all 27 bindings pass against the rebuilt v1.22.0 executable. Generated contracts match 62 operations and 232 routes.

Latest commit `f19f27a` includes the reviewed main merges and the measured coverage baseline. All seven workflows pass on that commit after its push: the [CI/CD pipeline](https://github.com/link-assistant/router/actions/runs/37972939145), downstream operations/contracts, benchmarks, fuzzing, real-client capture, Docker runtime build and Linux/macOS soak. The pipeline passes Linux, macOS and Windows tests and the dependent package build. The v1.22.0 documentation tests, independent Rust consumer and strict documentation checks also pass locally. Fresh instrumented coverage passes at 79138 / 91051 lines (86.916124%); its saved job log records the passing gate at `ci-logs/coverage-f19f27a-113965790820.log:7960` and the counts at line 7961. The committed 86.910633% baseline remains unchanged under the existing tolerance.

The earlier [instrumented run](https://github.com/link-assistant/router/actions/runs/37965002363) measured 79133 / 91051 lines (86.910633%). Its tests, floor and ratchet passed, but the reviewability check required committing the increased baseline: `Coverage changed the baseline. Commit coverage-baseline.txt so the ratchet update is reviewable.` The preserved job log records the measurement at `ci-logs/coverage-3a80d38-113956392542.log:7961` and the error at line 7994. The downloaded report advances the committed baseline through the existing checker; all eight coverage-policy tests pass. Coverage floors, tolerance, exception policy and test discovery are unchanged. Investigation notes and reproducing commands are in `experiments/issue-725/`; verbose logs remain in `ci-logs/`.

issue.title: JavaScript-first Router with full Rust parity via meta-language translation; bulk sub-agent drafting with one CI/CD push gate; Rust CI/CD starts only after JavaScript CI/CD passes
issue.body:
## Goal

Make Router development fast and light on the machines that run it:

1. **JavaScript first.** Every feature is implemented and tested in JavaScript first, and the Rust code is produced from it by automated translation through [link-foundation/meta-language](https://github.com/link-foundation/meta-language).
2. **Router gets a native JavaScript implementation with full feature parity** with the Rust one, enforced in CI like meta-language's parity gate. Today `packages/javascript` (`@link-assistant/router`) is a wrapper that runs the Rust binary (`ROUTER_BIN`), not an implementation.
3. **Bulk changes with sub-agents, and one push gate.** Several sub-agents draft all requirements in bulk. Exactly **one** sub-agent owns `git push`: it watches CI/CD, drafts the fixes for **all** failures of the last run, and pushes only once they are all drafted.
4. **Rust CI/CD cannot start until JavaScript CI/CD has fully passed.**

**Scope: this is the rule for all big Rust projects, not only Router.** Wherever a project has a lot of Rust code, development is JavaScript first, with a native JavaScript implementation at full parity, Rust produced by meta-language translation, a single CI/CD push gate, and Rust CI/CD gated on green JavaScript CI/CD. Router is where it is set up and proven first. Requirement 8 carries it to the other repositories.

## Evidence 1: latest unfinished pull requests with a lot of Rust

CI runs counted with `gh run list --branch <head>` on 2026-10-10.

| PR | Size | Commits | CI on the branch |
|---|---|---|---|
| link-foundation/meta-language#201 (draft) | +134,131 / −5,667 | 58 | `CI`: **44 runs, 0 green**, 25 failed, **19 cancelled** |
| link-foundation/relative-meta-logic#184 (draft) | +400,307 / −9,680 | 100+ | `issue-183-acceptance` **0/15 green**; `formal-corpus` 5 failed, `tests` 4 failed |
| link-assistant/formal-ai#1188 | +1,410,501 / −200,572 | 100+ | `CI/CD Pipeline` **0/11 green**, `Layered CI` **0/12**, `Coverage` 0/11 (5 cancelled), `Question necessity ratchet` 7 failed |
| link-assistant/router#749 (draft, for #724) | +15,086 / −388 | 33 | `CI/CD Pipeline` **3/18 green**, 9 failed, **5 cancelled** |

Pattern: many small pushes, each one starting the whole matrix and cancelling the previous run. Most runs are red or cancelled, so a full green run is rare even after dozens of pushes. The same workflows are re-run for every push while fixes arrive one at a time.

What already works and should be reused:

- **meta-language**: Rust and JavaScript side by side with a data-driven parity gate (`parity/language-features.json` + `js/scripts/check-js-rust-parity.mjs`), run by both `rust.yml` and `js.yml`, so changing one language without the other fails CI. Translation capabilities and boundaries are documented in `docs/four-language-contracts.md` and `docs/translation-rules.md`.
- **relative-meta-logic**: a dedicated `parity` workflow (15/15 green on #184) next to the Rust/JS jobs.
- **formal-ai**: "JS server parity" in #1188, and the associative stack in `docs/associative-tech-stack.md`.

## Evidence 2: what Rust builds cost on the agent host (2026-10-09 incident)

Router tasks (#724, #725, #727, #728), each in a hive-mind task container with a 2.92 GiB memory limit on an 11.7 GB / 6 CPU host:

- `rustc`/`clippy-driver` were OOM-killed inside the containers again and again: #724 ×5, #725 ×3, #727 ×2, #728 ×2 (kernel `Memory cgroup out of memory`). The agents had to write their own workarounds (`experiments/issue-719/bounded-build.py`, `ROUTER_BUILD_RSS_LIMIT_MIB=2450`, `target/local-unit-shards`, a copied `target/debug-initial`).
- `target/` per task: **17–30 GiB** (#724: 21.2 GiB old + 11.5 GiB resumed work dir; #727: 17.2 GiB; #728: 8.6 + 2.2 GiB). One task's writable layer reached 35.7 GiB, almost all of it `target/` and `~/.cargo/registry`. `target/semver-checks` alone was 1 GiB.
- A Rust build kept one task at about 110–135% CPU for hours; #724 (PR #749) has been running for 8+ hours.
- Disk use from these builds made recovery snapshots 46–63 GB per task and contributed to the disk filling up (link-assistant/hive-mind#2889).

Nearly all of that load is local Rust compilation. JavaScript tests need no compile step and a fraction of the memory and disk.

## Requirements

1. **Case study.** Collect the experience of the PRs above, and of the other Rust-heavy repositories (link-foundation/link-cli, link-foundation/links-notation, link-foundation/start, link-assistant/calculator), in `docs/case-studies/issue-{id}`: what made CI green, what caused repeated red/cancelled runs, how parity is enforced, and what translation through meta-language supports today. Turn the results into the rules below.
2. **Native JavaScript Router with full parity.** Implement Router's logic natively in JavaScript (Node 20+ and Bun), not as a wrapper around the binary: configuration, routing, cooldowns, accounts/tokens, OpenAI/Anthropic-compatible endpoints, CLI and every operation in `docs/integration/operations.md`. Add a parity manifest and checker on the meta-language model (`parity/…json` listing each feature with its JavaScript and Rust implementation and evidence), and shared fixtures/golden tests that both implementations must pass. Keep the existing wrapper package working, or merge it into the native package, without breaking downstream users.
3. **JavaScript first, Rust by translation.** New features and fixes land in JavaScript first, with tests. The Rust code is generated from the JavaScript source through meta-language translation, plus a regenerate-and-diff check, so generated Rust cannot drift. Where meta-language cannot translate a construct yet, report it to link-foundation/meta-language with a minimal example, and keep the hand-written Rust for that part small and listed in the parity manifest.
4. **Sub-agent workflow with a single push gate.** Document it in `CONTRIBUTING.md` and the agent instructions (`AGENTS.md`/`CLAUDE.md`), and report what solve needs to support it to link-assistant/hive-mind:
   - **Drafting sub-agents** work in parallel on the full list of requirements and produce bulk drafts. They never push.
   - **One CI/CD sub-agent** is the only one allowed to push. It monitors the CI/CD runs of the branch, collects every failure of the latest run (all jobs, all logs), and has fixes drafted for all of them. It pushes **once**, when all of those fixes and the pending drafts are in, never fix by fix. It never pushes while a run is still in progress on the same commit range, so runs are not cancelled.
   - Before the push it runs the JavaScript checks locally (fast), and never full local Rust builds unless a Rust-only change requires it.
5. **Minimal local load.** Local and agent-container development runs JavaScript tests only by default. If Rust has to be built locally: one shared, bounded `CARGO_TARGET_DIR`, `CARGO_INCREMENTAL=0`, reduced debug info, `-j` limited to the container's CPU/memory, and old artifacts pruned (`cargo-sweep` or equivalent). No per-work-dir 20–30 GiB `target/`.
6. **Rust CI/CD is gated on fully green JavaScript CI/CD.** It must be impossible to start any Rust job until the JavaScript stage has passed for the same commit:
   - One entry workflow whose Rust jobs `needs:` every JavaScript job (lint, tests, parity, translation regenerate-and-diff). Or separate Rust workflows triggered only by `workflow_run` with `conclusion == 'success'` of the JavaScript workflow and the same `head_sha`, with no `push`/`pull_request` triggers of their own.
   - A cancelled, skipped or partially successful JavaScript run must not start Rust. Path filters must not let a Rust-only change skip the JavaScript gate: the parity and translation checks always run.
   - Branch protection requires both stages. A per-branch `concurrency` group without cancel-in-progress for the Rust stage, so a gated Rust run is not thrown away by the next push.
   - A CI check that fails if any workflow can start Rust jobs without the JavaScript gate.
7. **Measure it.** Report before/after for a typical feature PR: pushes per PR, CI runs per PR (green/failed/cancelled), CI minutes, time to first fully green run, and peak local RSS/disk of an agent task.
8. **Apply it everywhere.** Write the approach as a reusable standard: the workflow gate (`needs:`/`workflow_run`), the parity manifest and checker, the translation regenerate-and-diff check, and the agent rules. Put it in the shared CI/CD templates (link-foundation/rust-ai-driven-development-pipeline-template and link-foundation/js-ai-driven-development-pipeline-template) and in link-assistant/hive-mind `docs/CI-CD-BEST-PRACTICES.md`. Then open one issue per big Rust repository (at least link-assistant/formal-ai, link-foundation/meta-language, link-foundation/relative-meta-logic, link-foundation/link-cli, link-foundation/links-notation, link-foundation/start, link-assistant/calculator) to adopt it, each linking back here.
9. **Audit every mentioned repository and file issues for missing best practices.** For link-assistant/router itself and each repository in requirement 8, compare it against this standard, the two pipeline templates and `docs/CI-CD-BEST-PRACTICES.md`, and open an issue **in that repository** for every missing or broken best practice that no open issue already covers. Each issue needs evidence (files, workflows, run counts) and testable requirements, and links back here. The checklist:
   - native JavaScript implementation and a parity manifest plus checker run in CI for both languages;
   - Rust generated from JavaScript through meta-language, with a regenerate-and-diff check;
   - no Rust job can start before the JavaScript stage passes for the same commit, and no path filter bypasses the gate;
   - `concurrency` groups, and cancelled runs wasted by push-per-fix;
   - Rust build load: cargo profile/config, CI caching, pruning old artifacts;
   - agent instructions (`AGENTS.md`/`CLAUDE.md`/`CONTRIBUTING.md`) for bulk drafting sub-agents with a single push gate;
   - differences from the templates (pinned actions, release/publish flow, link checks, security scans, false-positive/negative guards);
   - recurring failures on the default branch (for example a broken release job);
   - stale open pull requests.

Related: link-assistant/hive-mind#2889 (snapshot disk usage), link-assistant/hive-mind#2892 (OOM reporting), link-foundation/disk-space-saviour#36 (cargo-semver-checks cache).

---

We need to download all logs and data related about the issue to this repository, make sure we compile that data to `./docs/case-studies/issue-{id}` folder, and use it to do deep case study analysis (also make sure to search online for additional facts and data), in which we will reconstruct timeline/sequence of events, list of each and all requirements from the issue, find root causes of the each problem, and propose possible solutions and solution plans for each requirement (we should also check known existing components/libraries, that solve similar problem or can help in solutions).

If there is not enough data to find actual root cause, add debug output and verbose mode if not present, that will allow us to find root cause on next iteration.

If issue related to any other repository/project, where we can report issues on GitHub, please do so. Each issue must contain reproducible examples, workarounds and suggestions for fix the issue in code. Also double check to fully apply requirements to entire codebase, so if we have issue in multiple places, it should be fixed in all them.

Please plan and execute everything in this single pull request, you have unlimited time and context, as context auto-compacts and you can continue indefinitely, until it is each and every requirement fully addressed, and everything is totally done.

issue.title: Containers killed by a Docker daemon restart are reported as OOM-killed

repository.name: hive-mind
repository.description: The AI that controls AIs to do the automation of automation.

issue.body:
## Incident context (2026-10-09)

Host: Ubuntu 24.04, 6 CPU, 11.7 GB RAM, 193 GB disk, Docker 29.6.1 with the containerd image store (`overlayfs` snapshotter), live-restore disabled. Root container `hive-mind` (DinD variant, `--restart unless-stopped`) runs `hive-telegram-bot`; tasks run as `$ --isolated docker` containers from `konard/hive-mind-dind:2.34.0`. hive-mind 2.34.0, start-command 0.35.4.

At 12:11:39 UTC the kernel OOM-killed the **host dockerd** (7.3 GB RSS, caused by ~22 concurrent `docker diff` calls from a disk-cleanup tool test suite run inside the root container — link-foundation/disk-space-saviour#22). systemd restarted dockerd, which SIGKILLed every running container (exit 137): the root `hive-mind` container and four `/codex` solve tasks for link-assistant/router#724, #725, #727, #728. The root container was started again manually at 13:31 UTC; the bot then ran its built-in kill recovery.

## Problem

Containers that were killed because the **Docker daemon restarted** are reported as out-of-memory kills:

```
$ --list → "exitCode": 137, "oomKilled": true,
           "exitReason": "memory-exhaustion (cgroup-oom-killer)",
           "memoryExhaustedReason": "Docker reported State.OOMKilled=true"
bot      → EVENT session_completed {"sessionName":"…","exitCode":137,"status":"oom-killed"}
```

What actually happened (host journal, times CEST):
```
14:11:39 kernel: Out of memory: Killed process 823 (dockerd) total-vm:13940936kB, anon-rss:7302520kB …   ← global OOM, not a container cgroup
14:11:41 systemd: docker.service: Main process exited, code=killed, status=9/KILL
14:11:45 dockerd: Loading containers: start.
14:11:55 dockerd: Container failed to exit within 10s of signal 15 - using the force container=8bde925c…
```
Earlier that day each task container had a few cgroup OOM kills of a **child** process (`rustc`/`clippy-driver` hitting the container's 2.9 GiB limit: 724 ×5, 725 ×3, 727 ×2, 728 ×2) that the container survived. Docker's `State.OOMKilled` is set once *any* OOM kill happened during the container's lifetime, so it stayed `true`; the exit 137 itself came from dockerd force-killing the containers while restoring after its own crash. hive-mind and start-command read `OOMKilled=true` + 137 as "the container was OOM-killed". The root container (no OOM events, `OOMKilled=false`) was killed the same way at the same second.

The wrong diagnosis has consequences: Telegram and PR text say the task ran out of memory, and it steers any memory-based policy (smaller limits, refusing to resume).

## Suggested fix

- Before reporting `oom-killed`, check that the OOM kill hit the container's main process near `FinishedAt` (kernel journal `oom-kill:… task_memcg=…<container id>` with the init/solve pid, or `memory.events` changing at exit), not an earlier child-process kill the container survived. Detect a daemon restart (dockerd start time later than the container's `FinishedAt`, or many containers finished in the same second) and report it as "killed by Docker daemon restart (dockerd was OOM-killed / restarted)".
- Report the upstream part to link-foundation/start for `$ --list`'s `exitReason`.
- Docs: recommend `"live-restore": true` in `/etc/docker/daemon.json` for hosts running hive-mind, so a dockerd crash or upgrade no longer kills the root container and every task (it would have prevented this whole incident).

---

We need to download all logs and data related about the issue to this repository, make sure we compile that data to `./docs/case-studies/issue-{id}` folder, and use it to do deep case study analysis (also make sure to search online for additional facts and data), in which we will reconstruct timeline/sequence of events, list of each and all requirements from the issue, find root causes of the each problem, and propose possible solutions and solution plans for each requirement (we should also check known existing components/libraries, that solve similar problem or can help in solutions).

If there is not enough data to find actual root cause, add debug output and verbose mode if not present, that will allow us to find root cause on next iteration.

If issue related to any other repository/project, where we can report issues on GitHub, please do so. Each issue must contain reproducible examples, workarounds and suggestions for fix the issue in code. Also double check to fully apply requirements to entire codebase, so if we have issue in multiple places, it should be fixed in all them.

Please plan and execute everything in this single pull request, you have unlimited time and context, as context auto-compacts and you can continue indefinitely, until it is each and every requirement fully addressed, and everything is totally done.
